stories.title: Trouble at Sea Pushes Oil Prices Past $100
stories.headline_kid: Fighting near a busy sea route made oil prices jump — and that could make things pricier for us in Singapore.
summary: A group called the Houthis, who control part of Yemen, has been taking over more towns along the coast near the Red Sea. This week they captured a port city called Mocha and moved further along the coastline. The Red Sea is like a busy highway for ships — lots of oil tankers use it to carry oil from the Middle East to the rest of the world.

Because people are worried that ships might not be able to pass safely, the price of oil jumped a lot. On Thursday, the price went above US$100 for one barrel of oil (a barrel is just a big container used to measure oil) — that's a really high price compared to recent months.

Singapore doesn't have its own oil wells, so we buy oil from other countries to make petrol, run buses, and even make everyday plastic items. When oil becomes more expensive to buy, it can eventually mean higher petrol prices, pricier bus and taxi rides, and even costlier flights.

This is still developing, and experts are watching closely to see if it gets better or worse. For now, families might notice small increases in transport costs over the coming weeks if the situation continues.

lenses.me: If your parents drive you to school, petrol getting pricier could mean your family thinks more about how often they use the car.
lenses.family: Grocery shopping, bus fares and flight tickets could slowly become a bit more expensive if oil stays costly.
lenses.friends: Your friends' families who travel by car or take Grab/taxi a lot may feel the pinch first.
lenses.nation: Singapore imports all its oil, so world oil prices directly affect prices here — from petrol to plastic products.
lenses.world: This shows how fighting in one part of the world (Yemen) can ripple out and affect ordinary people's wallets everywhere, including us.

stories.title: Singapore Reaches Out to Nearly 100 Singaporeans After Nepal Disaster
stories.headline_kid: Our government has been checking on almost 100 Singaporeans caught up in the terrible floods in Nepal and Tibet.
summary: You may remember that huge floods hit Nepal and nearby Tibet last week, sweeping away roads and homes. Singapore's Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) says it has now reached out to nearly 100 Singaporeans and Permanent Residents who were in the area when the disaster struck.

Sadly, nine Singaporeans are still missing. Foreign Affairs Minister Vivian Balakrishnan said the government is helping the families of these missing people, offering support and information as search efforts continue.

MFA officers have been working hard to contact everyone who might have been affected, making sure they are safe and helping them get home if needed. This kind of help for citizens overseas is called 'consular assistance' — it's like our country's way of looking after Singaporeans wherever they travel.
This is a sad and worrying time for the families involved, and many Singaporeans are hoping for good news soon. It's a reminder that our government works to protect Singaporeans even far from home.

lenses.me: If you ever travel abroad with your family, know that Singapore's government has a system to help citizens caught in emergencies.
lenses.family: Parents might feel reassured knowing MFA actively checks on Singaporeans during overseas disasters.
lenses.friends: Some classmates may have relatives or family friends who travel to Nepal for trekking — this news might feel personal to them.
lenses.nation: It shows how Singapore takes care of its people no matter where they are in the world.
lenses.world: It highlights how natural disasters can suddenly put travellers from many countries in danger, not just locals.

stories.title: China's New Travel Rules Kick In Next Week — Should You Worry?
stories.headline_kid: China is putting new rules about entering and leaving the country into writing — but tour guides say travellers shouldn't panic.
summary: Starting Sep 15, China will have new 'exit-entry' rules — these are rules about who can come into the country and who can leave. Mostly, these rules just write down things that were already happening, but they also give Chinese authorities more power to step in during sensitive situations involving people crossing the border.

Tour operators and travellers, including Singaporean tour groups, say they aren't too worried. One Singapore tour leader recently even got invited to witness a wedding while leading a group trip in Xinjiang, showing that everyday travel experiences remain warm and friendly.

Experts who study China say the new rules could matter more in unusual or 'sensitive' cases — for example, if someone is involved in a dispute or investigation. For most tourists just visiting to sightsee, shop, or try local food, daily life and travel plans should stay much the same.
If your family is planning a holiday to China, it's still a good idea to check the latest travel advisories, but there's no reason for alarm based on what experts are saying so far.

lenses.me: If your family visits China for a holiday, these rules probably won't change your trip much.
lenses.family: Parents planning trips to China should just double-check visa and entry requirements before flying.
lenses.friends: Classmates whose families travel often to China for business or visiting relatives might hear their parents talk about this news.
lenses.nation: Singapore has close travel and trade ties with China, so understanding its rules helps Singaporean travellers and businesses plan smoothly.
lenses.world: It shows how countries update their laws over time, sometimes giving themselves more control over how people move across borders.

stories.title: Mount Fuji's Hiking Season Ends with a Landslide
stories.headline_kid: Japan's most famous mountain closed its hiking season with heavy rain, mist and a landslide!
summary: Mount Fuji, Japan's tallest and most famous mountain, just wrapped up its summer hiking season — but not quietly. On the very last day, heavy rain and strong winds battered the mountain, and a landslide hit a car park near the trails.

Three vehicles belonging to mountain workers were partially buried by the landslide. Two people needed to be rescued during the wild weather, though thankfully the situation was brought under control.

Mount Fuji is a very popular spot for hikers from all over the world, including many Singaporean tourists who dream of climbing it or seeing its beautiful snowcap. Every year, the mountain only opens for climbing during a few summer months because the weather gets too dangerous otherwise.

This incident is a good reminder that even famous, beautiful places can turn dangerous quickly when the weather changes — which is why hikers always need to follow safety rules and check forecasts before heading up any mountain.

lenses.me: If you love mountains or nature trips, this story shows why checking the weather before an outdoor adventure really matters.
lenses.family: Families planning a Japan holiday around Mount Fuji should note the hiking season is now closed until next summer.
lenses.friends: Friends who enjoy hiking or camping can learn why safety rules exist even on 'safe-looking' trails.
lenses.nation: Many Singaporeans travel to Japan every year, so weather and safety updates there are useful for trip planning.
lenses.world: It's a reminder that extreme weather events, possibly linked to changing climate patterns, can affect even well-known, well-managed places.

stories.title: Singapore's Shannon Tan Chases Her Big Golf Dream
stories.headline_kid: Singaporean golfer Shannon Tan is aiming for a spot on one of the world's toughest golf tours!
summary: Shannon Tan, a talented golfer from Singapore, has her eyes set on earning a card for the LPGA Tour — one of the biggest and most competitive women's golf tours in the world — for the 2027 season.

This year, she has already shown she's got what it takes, finishing in the top 10 five times on the Ladies European Tour. That's a fantastic result, showing she can compete with some of the best golfers around.

Getting an LPGA Tour card is a big deal. It means a golfer has proven she's good enough to regularly play against the world's top players in major tournaments. For a Singaporean athlete, achieving this would be a huge milestone for local sport.

Shannon's journey is a great example of hard work paying off. She trains hard, travels for tournaments, and keeps improving — showing young Singaporeans that with dedication, you really can chase big dreams on the world stage.

lenses.nation: Shannon Tan flying Singapore's flag on a major international golf tour would be a proud moment for the whole country.
lenses.world: It shows how small nations like Singapore can still produce athletes who compete at the very top level globally.
